verseByVerse.commentary:
Four more, and they come in two pairs that describe how a man behaves when things are difficult.

'Not a drunkard' — the word is literally one who lingers beside wine. The Bible does not forbid wine and this letter will shortly tell Timothy to take a little for his stomach (5:23). What is in view is the man whose relationship with drink has become the governing fact about his evenings.

'Not violent but gentle.' The first word means a striker — one who hits people. That such a thing needed saying about candidates for church office tells us something about the world Paul was working in. Against it he sets epieikes, that untranslatable word from Philippians 4:5: the man who does not insist on the last inch of what he is owed, who knows when the strict letter would do an injustice.

'Not quarrelsome' — not a fighter, and here it means with words rather than fists. Given chapter 1, this is pointed. Ephesus was full of vain discussion and confident assertion, and it would be easy to conclude that what the church needed was a leader who could out-argue them. Paul says the opposite. A man who enjoys the fight is disqualified from the office, however right he happens to be.

'Not a lover of money.' Money runs through this letter — the false teachers imagining godliness is a means of gain (6:5), the love of money as a root of all kinds of evils (6:10), the rich charged not to be haughty (6:17). A man who loves money will eventually be bought, and everyone will find out what the price was.

Notice what these four have in common. Drink, violence, arguing, money — each is a way of handling pressure or appetite badly, and each is invisible to a congregation until it is far too late. That is why the qualifications are for character rather than performance. You can assess a man's preaching in twenty minutes; these take years to see.

verseByVerse.quote: He must manage his own household well, with all dignity keeping his children submissive, for if someone does not know how to manage his own household, how will he care for God's church?
verseByVerse.commentary:
'He must manage his own household well, with all dignity keeping his children submissive.' Then the reason, put as a question that answers itself: 'for if someone does not know how to manage his own household, how will he care for God's church?'

The argument runs from lesser to greater, and it assumes something the modern church often does not: that home and congregation are the same kind of thing. Both are households. The word for 'manage' is the same in both halves of the sentence, and Paul will call the church 'the household of God' eleven verses later (v.15). A man who cannot run the small one cannot be handed the large one.

Note the verb Paul chooses for the church, though, because it changes at the crucial moment. He does not ask how a man will manage God's church. He asks how he will care for it — the same verb used of the Samaritan taking charge of the wounded man at the inn (Luke 10:34-35). Managing a household qualifies a man for something warmer than management.

'With all dignity' probably describes the father's manner rather than the children's — the household is ordered without being harsh. A house kept in line by fear would meet the letter of this requirement and fail its spirit entirely, and Paul has already ruled out the violent man in verse 3.

This requirement has caused a great deal of pain, and it should be handled honestly. It is not a guarantee that a good father's children will all believe; Scripture nowhere promises that, and godly parents have watched children walk away since Genesis. What Paul is describing is the present ordering of a household still under a man's charge — whether his home is a place of evident care and order, or whether it is visibly out of control.

And the principle reaches past elders to everyone. The place where a person's real character is known is the house he lives in. Public competence is easy to manufacture for a few hours a week; nobody sustains a performance in front of the people who see him tired.

verseByVerse.quote: He must not be a recent convert, or he may become puffed up with conceit and fall into the condemnation of the devil. Moreover, he must be well thought of by outsiders, so that he may not fall into disgrace, into a snare of the devil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two final requirements, and each is guarded by a warning about the devil — the only two places in the list where Paul explains what happens if you get it wrong.

'He must not be a recent convert.' The word is neophytos, newly planted — our neophyte. The danger is named exactly: 'or he may become puffed up with conceit and fall into the condemnation of the devil.'

'Puffed up' is an inflation word — swollen with air, larger than the substance warrants. And 'the condemnation of the devil' most likely means the condemnation the devil incurred: the sin that ruined him was pride, and a man promoted before he is ready is being walked along the same road. Give a new believer standing and authority quickly, and you may not be honouring him. You may be endangering him.

This is a hard rule for a church in a hurry, especially a young or growing one that needs leaders now. Paul's answer is that the shortage is not a reason to promote early, because the cost of doing so falls on the man himself.

Then verse 7, and it is the most surprising qualification in the chapter: 'he must be well thought of by outsiders.'

The church does not get to assess its leaders on its own. Paul makes the opinion of non-Christians — neighbours, tradesmen, employers, the people who see the man when he is not being religious — a formal qualification for office. Not that they must approve of his beliefs; the gospel will always offend. But they must not be able to say he is dishonest, or cruel, or unreliable.

The danger is 'disgrace' and 'a snare of the devil' — a trap, the word for a bird-snare. A leader with a bad reputation outside the church is already caught: everything he says about Christ is discounted by the people who know what he is like, and he cannot free himself by arguing. Which is a fair question for any Christian to ask, not only an elder. What would your neighbours say about you if the subject came up?

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Deacons likewise must be dignified, not double-tongued, not addicted to much wine, not greedy for dishonest gain (v.8), holding the mystery of the faith with a clear conscience (v.9); and they are to be tested first, then serve if they prove blameless (v.10). The women likewise are to be dignified, not slanderers, sober-minded, faithful in all things (v.11). Deacons are each to be a one-woman man, managing children and household well (v.12) — for those who serve well gain a good standing and great confidence in the faith that is in Christ Jesus (v.13).
verseByVerse.theology:
Wives, or Women Deacons?

Verse 11 is genuinely ambiguous. The Greek gynaikas means either women or wives — the language does not distinguish — and there is no possessive pronoun in the text. The ESV takes it as deacons' wives, since the verse sits inside the deacon paragraph and verse 12 returns to the men.

The other reading, women serving as deacons, has real support: 'likewise' introduces each new group in this chapter (vv.8, 11) as though a third category is named; the qualities match the deacons' own point for point; and no equivalent verse appears about overseers' wives, which would be odd if wives were the subject. Paul also calls Phoebe a diakonos of the church at Cenchreae (Rom 16:1). The passage does not settle it, and honest readers should say so. What is not in doubt is that the same standard of character is required either way.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Notice what is missing from the deacons' list: 'able to teach'. That single skill separated the overseer, and its absence here defines the deacon's work — he serves rather than teaches, while everything else is just as demanding. The office appears to descend from Acts 6, where seven were appointed over the distribution of food. The vices named fit the job exactly: 'double-tongued' is a precise hazard for men moving between households hearing everybody's business, and 'greedy for dishonest gain' matters when relief funds pass through your hands with no ledger anybody checks. 'Not slanderers' in verse 11 uses diabolos, the devil's own title, which should sober anyone who has enjoyed passing something on.

Now: Verse 10's order is the one most churches reverse. Test first, then appoint — and the testing is by time, not examination (dokimazo, the assayer's word). Appointing a man and finding out afterwards is how most congregations actually proceed and how most of them come to grief. And verse 13 attaches a striking promise to practical service: not promotion but parrhesia, the boldness to speak freely. A man who has carried food to widows for years ends up with a settledness in the faith that study alone does not produce. Serving well does something to the server.

verseByVerse.quote: Deacons likewise must be dignified, not double-tongued, not addicted to much wine, not greedy for dishonest gain. They must hold the mystery of the faith with a clear conscience. And let them also be tested first; then let them serve as deacons if they prove themselves blameless.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Deacons likewise.' The word ties the second office to the first — same seriousness, different function. Diakonos means servant, and the office appears to descend from Acts 6, where seven men were appointed to handle the distribution of food so that the apostles could give themselves to prayer and the word.

Notice at once what is missing from this list. There is no 'able to teach'. That single skill separated the overseer, and its absence here defines the deacon's work: he serves rather than teaches. Everything else — the character, the testing, the blamelessness — is just as demanding.

Four negatives. 'Dignified' first, the same word used of the overseer's household manner. 'Not double-tongued' — literally two-worded, saying one thing here and another there. It is a precise hazard for men who move between households collecting and distributing, hearing everybody's business. A deacon who repeats in one house what he heard in another destroys the trust the job runs on.

'Not addicted to much wine' and 'not greedy for dishonest gain' — and the second is exact for the office. Deacons handled money for the poor. The phrase means eager for shameful profit, and the temptation is obvious: funds passing through your hands with no ledger anybody checks.

Then verse 9, which is the positive at the centre: 'They must hold the mystery of the faith with a clear conscience.' Deacons are not required to expound the faith, but they must hold it — and hold it with a conscience that is clean. That phrase has already appeared twice (1:5, 19), and it is the letter's steady concern. A man may distribute bread faultlessly while carrying something unresolved, and Paul will not have it.

And verse 10 gives the procedure: 'let them also be tested first; then let them serve.' Not tested by an examination but by time — the verb is the assayer's word again, dokimazo, proving metal. Paul's order is: observe the man, then appoint him. The reverse order — appoint him and find out afterwards — is how most churches actually do it, and it is how most of them come to grief.

verseByVerse.quote: Their wives likewise must be dignified, not slanderers, but sober-minded, faithful in all things. Let deacons each be the husband of one wife, managing their children and their own households well. For those who serve well as deacons gain a good standing for themselves and also great confidence in the faith that is in Christ Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Their wives likewise must be dignified, not slanderers, but sober-minded, faithful in all things.'

The Greek word is simply gynaikas, which means either women or wives — the language does not distinguish, and there is no possessive pronoun in the text. So the verse is genuinely ambiguous, and the choice matters.

Two readings are held by serious Christians. The ESV takes it as deacons' wives, on the ground that the verse sits inside the deacon paragraph and verse 12 returns to the men. The other takes it as women who serve as deacons, and has real support: the word 'likewise' introduces each new group in this chapter (v.8, v.11) as though a third category is being named; the qualities listed match the deacons' own point for point; and no equivalent verse appears about overseers' wives, which would be strange if wives were the subject. Paul also calls Phoebe a diakonos of the church at Cenchreae (Rom 16:1).

The passage does not settle it, and honest readers should say so. What is not in doubt is that the same standard of character is required either way, and that the qualities are the ones this letter keeps returning to.

'Not slanderers' is the counterpart to the deacons' 'not double-tongued' — the word is diabolos, the same word used of the devil, whose name means accuser. Careless talk about people is given the devil's own title, which should sober anyone who has ever enjoyed passing something on.

Then verse 13, and it is a promise rather than a requirement: 'those who serve well as deacons gain a good standing for themselves and also great confidence in the faith.' Parrhesia — the boldness of a man who can speak freely, the word used of the apostles before the council.

That is a striking thing to attach to practical service. Paul does not promise deacons promotion; he promises them assurance. A man who has carried food to widows for years, quietly and honestly, ends up with a settledness in the faith that no amount of study produces on its own. Serving well does something to the server.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul states the letter's purpose: he hopes to come soon, but writes in case he is delayed (v.14), so that they may know how to behave in the household of God — the church of the living God, a pillar and buttress of the truth (v.15).

And then the chapter of overseers, deacons, wine and money opens into a hymn: great indeed is the mystery of godliness — he was manifested in the flesh, vindicated by the Spirit, seen by angels, proclaimed among the nations, believed on in the world, taken up in glory (v.16).
verseByVerse.theology:
Pillar and Buttress — and Which Way Round

Everyone in Ephesus knew what a pillar was. The temple of Artemis had well over a hundred of them, sixty feet high, one of the seven wonders of the world. Paul takes the architectural vocabulary of the most famous building in Asia and applies it to congregations meeting in houses — and calls their God the living God, an adjective with teeth in a city whose great temple housed an image that could not move.

But get the relation the right way round, because it is often inverted. The church does not create the truth or authenticate it. A pillar does not make the roof; it holds it up where people can see it. The truth stands on its own, and the church's task is to hold it visibly in place — precisely what the false teachers of chapter 1 were failing to do. That gives a congregation its shape: not primarily a service provider, a campaign or a community centre, but the structure by which the truth about God is held up in a town.

The hymn of verse 16 has six lines, each beginning with a verb, and every verb is passive. Christ is the subject throughout and the actor nowhere: God does all of it. 'Manifested in the flesh' means he existed before he appeared, and in real flesh — the line rules out both early errors at once. 'Vindicated by the Spirit' is the language of justification: condemned by a Roman court, he was declared to be in the right by a higher one.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The letter exists because of a contingency — Paul intends to come and may not. A good deal of Scripture came to us that way; he could not get to Thessalonica either, and we have two letters because of it. And 'household of God' is what chapter 3 has been building toward: the overseer must manage his own household because the church is one. A household in that world was not a nuclear family but an extended body — kin, servants, dependants — with an order to it and a head.

Now: Note the least likely pair in the hymn: 'proclaimed among the nations, believed on in the world.' The other lines are about Christ himself; these two are about what happened next, and they are the improbable part. A crucified provincial was announced to an empire, and people believed it — and Paul is writing to a church in Ephesus that exists because that line came true. Notice too where the hymn sits: straight after a chapter on wine, money, household management and reputation. The rules are not religious housekeeping. They exist so that the pillar stands straight and this can be seen from the street.

verseByVerse.quote: I hope to come to you soon, but I am writing these things to you so that, if I delay, you may know how one ought to behave in the household of God, which is the church of the living God, a pillar and buttress of the truth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'I hope to come to you soon, but I am writing these things to you so that, if I delay, you may know how one ought to behave in the household of God.'

Here is the letter's own statement of purpose, and the honesty of it should be noted. Paul intends to come. He may not. The letter exists because of a contingency, which is how a great deal of Scripture came to be written — Paul could not get to Thessalonica either, and we have two letters because of it.

'The household of God.' Everything in chapter 3 has been building here. The overseer must manage his own household because the church is one; the deacons serve in it; and now the whole is named. A household in that world was not a nuclear family but an extended body — kin, servants, dependants — with an order to it and a head. The church is that, and it is God's.

Then two further descriptions, and they lift the sentence enormously. 'The church of the living God' — and the adjective has teeth in Ephesus, whose great temple housed an image that could not move. And 'a pillar and buttress of the truth'.

Anyone in that city knew what a pillar was. The temple of Artemis had well over a hundred of them, sixty feet high, one of the seven wonders of the world. A pillar holds something up so it can be seen; a buttress is the foundation-support that keeps it from shifting. Paul takes the architectural vocabulary of the most famous building in Asia and applies it to a congregation meeting in houses.

Get the relation the right way round, though, because it is often inverted. The church does not create the truth or authenticate it. A pillar does not make the roof; it holds it up where people can see it. The truth stands on its own and the church's task is to hold it visibly in place — which is exactly what the false teachers of chapter 1 were failing to do.

And that gives the church's job a shape. A congregation is not primarily a service provider, a campaign, or a community centre. It is the structure by which the truth about God is held up in a town so that people can see it.

verseByVerse.quote: Great indeed, we confess, is the mystery of godliness: He was manifested in the flesh, vindicated by the Spirit, seen by angels, proclaimed among the nations, believed on in the world, taken up in glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Great indeed, we confess, is the mystery of godliness' — and then the sentence changes shape entirely. What follows is rhythmic, balanced, and almost certainly a hymn the churches sang. Paul quotes it whole.

Six lines, each beginning with a verb, and every one of them passive: he was manifested, vindicated, seen, proclaimed, believed on, taken up. Christ is the subject throughout and the actor nowhere. God is doing all of it.

'Manifested in the flesh' — he was manifested, which means he existed before he appeared. And in flesh: not a semblance, not a costume, but the real thing. The first line rules out the two errors the early church had to fight, that he was not truly divine and that he was not truly human.

'Vindicated by the Spirit' — the word is justified, declared to be in the right. He had been condemned by a Roman court and executed as a criminal; the resurrection by the Spirit was the higher court overturning the verdict.

'Seen by angels' — the unseen world watched. Angels appear at every hinge of his life: the announcement, the birth, the wilderness, Gethsemane, the empty tomb, the ascension. Peter says they long to look into these things (1 Pet 1:12).

'Proclaimed among the nations, believed on in the world' — and this is the astonishing pair, because it is the least likely thing on the list. The other lines are about him; these two are about what happened next. A crucified provincial was announced to the empire, and people believed it. Paul is writing to a church in Ephesus that exists because that line came true.

'Taken up in glory' — the ascension, and the hymn ends where he now is.

Notice where this sits. Paul has spent a chapter on overseers, deacons, wine, money, household management and reputation — the unglamorous machinery of a working church. Then he says: and this is what it is all for. The rules about drink and quarrelling are not religious housekeeping. They exist so that the pillar stands straight and this can be seen from the street.

3.text: <sup>1</sup>The saying is trustworthy: If anyone aspires to the office of overseer, he desires a noble task.<sup>2</sup>Therefore an overseer must be above reproach, the husband of one wife, sober-minded, self-controlled, respectable, hospitable, able to teach,<sup>3</sup>not a drunkard, not violent but gentle, not quarrelsome, not a lover of money.<sup>4</sup>He must manage his own household well, with all dignity keeping his children submissive,<sup>5</sup>for if someone does not know how to manage his own household, how will he care for God's church?<sup>6</sup>He must not be a recent convert, or he may become puffed up with conceit and fall into the condemnation of the devil.<sup>7</sup>Moreover, he must be well thought of by outsiders, so that he may not fall into disgrace, into a snare of the devil.<sup>8</sup>Deacons likewise must be dignified, not double-tongued, not addicted to much wine, not greedy for dishonest gain.<sup>9</sup>They must hold the mystery of the faith with a clear conscience.<sup>10</sup>And let them also be tested first; then let them serve as deacons if they prove themselves blameless.<sup>11</sup>Their wives likewise must be dignified, not slanderers, but sober-minded, faithful in all things.<sup>12</sup>Let deacons each be the husband of one wife, managing their children and their own households well.<sup>13</sup>For those who serve well as deacons gain a good standing for themselves and also great confidence in the faith that is in Christ Jesus.<sup>14</sup>I hope to come to you soon, but I am writing these things to you so that,<sup>15</sup>if I delay, you may know how one ought to behave in the household of God, which is the church of the living God, a pillar and buttress of the truth.<sup>16</sup>Great indeed, we confess, is the mystery of godliness: He was manifested in the flesh, vindicated by the Spirit, seen by angels, proclaimed among the nations, believed on in the world, taken up in glory.

4.title: A Good Servant of Christ Jesus
4.overview:
Chapter 4 brings the letter into sharp personal focus on Timothy himself. After addressing the congregation's prayer life and the church's officers, Paul now turns to the young pastor: here is what you must do, here is how you must live, here is what you must not neglect. The chapter is one of the richest pastoral training texts in the New Testament — a manual for the minister who wants to be 'a good servant of Christ Jesus.'

The chapter is framed by a warning (vv. 1–5) and a training programme (vv. 6–16). The warning is eschatological: the Spirit explicitly says that in later times some will depart from the faith. The signs are already visible in Ephesus — teachers who forbid marriage and require abstinence from foods that God created. The response is twofold: correct the false teaching with truth, and train yourself in godliness. Both activities — teaching and training — are the irreducible core of pastoral work.

verseByVerse.ref: 4:1–5 – Some Will Depart from the Faith
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The Spirit says expressly that in later times some will depart from the faith, devoting themselves to deceitful spirits and teachings of demons (v.1), through the insincerity of liars whose consciences are seared (v.2) — men who forbid marriage and require abstinence from foods God created to be received with thanksgiving by those who believe and know the truth (v.3).

Paul's answer is the doctrine of creation: everything God made is good, and nothing is to be rejected if received with thanksgiving (v.4), since it is made holy by the word of God and prayer (v.5).
verseByVerse.theology:
False Teaching That Restricts Rather Than Permits

The error at Ephesus is not what a modern reader predicts. It is ascetic — a religion marked by what it refuses. We assume false teaching will be permissive, letting people do what they want; Paul is dealing with the opposite, and it has been at least as common in church history: the teaching that impresses by how much it gives up. Behind it lay the durable idea that matter is the problem and spirituality means escaping the body, so the two most bodily things — marriage and food — had to go. The same instinct produced the Colossian error ('do not handle, do not taste, do not touch') and flowered into gnosticism in the next century.

Paul does not negotiate about how much asceticism is appropriate. He goes to Genesis 1, where God pronounces his work good six times and then very good — a verdict never withdrawn. The fall damaged the world's use, not its origin. And note the purpose clause: God created these things to be received. Declining a gift is not humility when the gift was made on purpose for you.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: 'Consciences seared' uses the verb for branding with a hot iron, and the picture is exact: scar tissue does not feel. These men have not lost their consciences but anaesthetised them, by going against them repeatedly until the nerve died — the same sequence as 1:19, where the conscience was rejected first and the faith followed it onto the rocks. Note too that the demonic works through entirely ordinary channels here: no possession, no spectacle, just men saying things they know to be untrue, in a normal voice, in a meeting.

Now: Verse 5 gives grace at the table a genuinely priestly weight — the most routine act of Christian domestic piety, the one children learn first and adults do on autopilot, actually sanctifies a common meal. And that is the practical answer to asceticism, harder to live than it sounds. The ascetic refuses the gift and feels holy. Paul's alternative is neither to refuse nor to grab, but to take it and say thank you — which requires thinking about God at the moment you are most likely to forget him, which is the moment you are enjoying something.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the Spirit expressly says that in later times some will depart from the faith by devoting themselves to deceitful spirits and teachings of demons, through the insincerity of liars whose consciences are seared,
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Now the Spirit expressly says.' The word means in so many words, explicitly, in plain terms. Paul is not inferring this from general principles; he is reporting something the Spirit has stated — whether through the prophets of the churches, or through a word given to him, or through what Jesus himself had taught about the last days.

'That in later times some will depart from the faith.' Not 'the last times' in the sense of a distant final period. In New Testament reckoning the later times had already begun with Christ's coming, and Paul plainly treats what follows as a present description of Ephesus. The prophecy is being fulfilled in the room.

'Depart from the faith' is apostesontai, from which we get apostasy — a standing away, a defection. And the mechanism is given: 'by devoting themselves to deceitful spirits and teachings of demons.'

That phrase needs reading carefully, because it says something the church often forgets. Paul does not treat false teaching as merely a human mistake — a clever man reasoning badly. He treats it as having a source behind the visible one. The men in Ephesus were not, so far as anyone could see, occultists; they were church people with opinions about genealogies and diet. Paul says there is something else in the room.

But note at once that the demonic works through entirely ordinary human channels: 'through the insincerity of liars.' No possession, no spectacle. Men saying things they know to be untrue, in a normal voice, in a meeting.

Then the terrible clause: 'whose consciences are seared.' The verb is the one used of branding with a hot iron, and the picture is exact. Scar tissue does not feel. These men have not lost their consciences; they have anaesthetised them, by the ordinary process of going against them repeatedly until the nerve dies.

Which is the same sequence as 1:19, where the conscience was rejected first and the faith went down after it. It is the letter's steady warning, and it should be taken personally. Nobody arrives at a seared conscience suddenly. It is done one small over-ruling at a time, and the frightening part is that by the end it does not hurt.

verseByVerse.quote: who forbid marriage and require abstinence from foods that God created to be received with thanksgiving by those who believe and know the truth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the actual content of the false teaching, and it is not what a modern reader would predict. These men 'forbid marriage and require abstinence from foods.'

Not licence. Restriction. The error at Ephesus was ascetic — a religion of renunciation, marked by what it refused. Register that, because we naturally assume false teaching will be permissive, the sort that lets people do what they want. Paul is dealing with the opposite, and it has been at least as common in church history: the teaching that impresses by how much it gives up.

Behind it lay an old and durable idea — that the material world is the problem, and that spirituality means getting free of the body. Marriage and food are the two most bodily things there are, so both had to go. The same instinct produced the teaching Paul attacks in Colossians ('do not handle, do not taste, do not touch') and would flower into full gnosticism in the next century.

Paul's answer is not a compromise about how much asceticism is appropriate. He goes straight to the doctrine of creation: these are 'foods that God created to be received with thanksgiving.'

That single clause dismantles the whole system. If the world is God's and he made these things deliberately, then refusing them is not superior spirituality — it is an insult to the giver. And note the purpose he names: God created them to be received. They were made for the taking. Declining a gift is not humility when the gift was made on purpose for you.

'By those who believe and know the truth.' The capacity to enjoy created things rightly belongs to people who know where they came from. An unbeliever can eat and marry; what he cannot do is receive them as gifts, because he does not know there is anyone to thank.

verseByVerse.quote: For everything created by God is good, and nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving, for it is made holy by the word of God and prayer.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'For everything created by God is good, and nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving.'

Paul is quoting Genesis 1, where God looks at what he has made and pronounces it good, six times, and then very good. That verdict has never been withdrawn. The fall damaged the world's use, not its origin; matter is not the problem, and a religion that treats the physical as inherently unspiritual is at odds with the first page of the Bible.

'Nothing is to be rejected.' The scope is total, and it is a striking thing for an apostle to write to a church under pressure to be more rigorous. But the condition matters and is not a formality: if it is received with thanksgiving. Thanksgiving is what turns consumption into worship. The same meal eaten with gratitude and eaten greedily are two different acts, and Paul's line is not between the things but between the receivings.

Then verse 5: 'for it is made holy by the word of God and prayer.' Two instruments, and both are ordinary. 'The word of God' most likely means Scripture — quite possibly the Genesis verdict just cited — and 'prayer' means grace at the table.

Sit with what that implies. Paul says that saying grace over a plate of food sanctifies it — sets it apart, makes it holy. The most routine act of Christian domestic piety, the one children learn first and adults do on autopilot, is here given a genuinely priestly weight. A common meal becomes a holy thing when it is received consciously from God's hand.

And that is the practical answer to asceticism, which is far harder to live than it sounds. The ascetic refuses the gift and feels holy. Paul's alternative is not to refuse and not to grab, but to take it and say thank you — which requires you to think about God at the moment you are most likely to forget him, which is the moment you are enjoying something.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Setting these things before the brothers makes Timothy a good servant of Christ Jesus, himself being nourished on the words of the faith (v.6). He is to have nothing to do with irreverent, old-womanish myths, and to train himself for godliness instead (v.7) — for bodily training profits a little, but godliness profits in every way, holding promise for this life and the life to come (v.8). That saying is trustworthy (v.9): to this end they toil and strive, with hope set on the living God, the Saviour of all people, especially of believers (v.10).

Command and teach these things (v.11). Let nobody look down on Timothy for his youth; let him instead be a pattern in speech, conduct, love, faith and purity (v.12). Until Paul comes, he is to devote himself to the public reading of Scripture, to exhortation and to teaching (v.13), not neglecting the gift given him by prophecy when the elders laid hands on him (v.14). He is to practise these things and live inside them, so that his progress is visible to all (v.15) — watching himself and his teaching closely, and persisting, for so he will save both himself and his hearers (v.16).
verseByVerse.theology:
Godliness Is Trained For

The verb in verse 7 is gymnaze — the gymnasium word, and every Greek city had one. Paul is not dismissing the body in verse 8; he has just spent five verses defending food and marriage against men who despised the physical, and he concedes that bodily training is of some value. The comparison is one of scope: the strongest body on earth is on a schedule, and training for godliness is the only regime whose results survive the body they were performed in.

Do not miss the first half of the promise either — godliness holds value for the present life, not only the next. Paul is not offering a religion that pays out solely after death; a life ordered toward God is better now, in the plain sense that self-control beats being ruled by appetite and a clear conscience sleeps better. He will guard this against men who imagined godliness was a means of gain (6:5), but he does not withdraw it.

Verse 10's 'Saviour of all people, especially of those who believe' cannot mean universal salvation — this chapter has just described men departing from the faith. The likeliest sense turns on the breadth of saviour, which covers preservation as well as eternal rescue: God sustains every living thing, sends rain on the just and the unjust, and gives every breath any human being draws. That is real saving activity and it reaches all — and especially, in a final sense, believers. One generosity running at two depths.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: 'Public reading of Scripture' comes first in verse 13 for a reason. Most Christians could not read and copies were scarce and costly; hearing the Bible meant one literate person standing and reading it aloud. Before explanation, before application — the text itself, read out. Read, explain, apply is the shape of Christian ministry in three words, and it has not changed. Note also who commissioned Timothy: a council of elders, plural. His ministry was neither self-generated nor conferred by Paul alone, which is exactly the thing to remember when the work is going badly.

Now: Paul's counsel to a young man being looked down on is striking for what it does not say. He does not tell Timothy to assert himself, invoke his commission or be tougher, and he does not tell the church to respect him. He tells him to be a typos — a stamp leaving its impression — in five areas running from the most visible to the least: speech, conduct, love, faith, purity. The last is private, and it is where the matter is actually decided. And note that verse 15 expects visible progress: a leader still obviously under construction, which is the opposite of the finished article who has arrived and now dispenses. A minister who cannot be seen growing teaches his people that growth stops somewhere.

verseByVerse.quote: If you put these things before the brothers, you will be a good servant of Christ Jesus, being trained in the words of the faith and of the good doctrine that you have followed. Have nothing to do with irreverent, silly myths. Rather train yourself for godliness;
verseByVerse.commentary:
'If you put these things before the brothers, you will be a good servant of Christ Jesus.' The word is diakonos, and Paul uses it of Timothy the way he uses it of himself. The way to be a good servant is to set these things before people — not to innovate, but to serve up what he has been given.

'Being trained in the words of the faith and of the good doctrine that you have followed.' The participle is present and continuous — Timothy is being nourished on this while he feeds others. A minister who has stopped being fed will shortly have nothing to serve.

Then verse 7, and the two halves make a single instruction. 'Have nothing to do with irreverent, silly myths.' The verb means refuse, decline, turn away from. And the adjective translated 'silly' is literally old-womanish — the sort of tale somebody's grandmother tells. It is a dismissive phrase, and deliberately so: Paul is denying these teachings the dignity of a refutation.

That is a real pastoral judgement and not laziness. Some error should be answered carefully; some should be declined. To argue is to concede that the thing is worth arguing about, and there are teachings whose only power is the seriousness with which opponents treat them. Timothy is not told to defeat the myths. He is told to walk past them.

'Rather train yourself for godliness.' The verb is gymnaze — the gymnasium word, which is where our word comes from, and every Greek city had one. It means the disciplined, repetitive, unglamorous work of an athlete in training.

Note the shape of the sentence: refuse that, and put the energy into this. Paul does not merely tell Timothy to avoid a distraction; he gives him somewhere to spend the effort. Godliness, on this account, is not a temperament some people are born with. It is trained for, the way a body is — by doing the same unremarkable things repeatedly, long past the point where they feel interesting.

verseByVerse.quote: for while bodily training is of some value, godliness is of value in every way, as it holds promise for the present life and also for the life to come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'While bodily training is of some value, godliness is of value in every way.' Paul continues the gymnasium image and makes a comparison — but read it carefully, because it is not the dismissal it is often taken for.

He does not say physical training is worthless. He says it is of some value, which is a genuine concession, and one you would not expect from a man supposedly hostile to the body. He has just spent five verses defending food and marriage against people who despised the physical. He is not about to turn round and despise it himself.

The comparison is one of scope. Bodily training profits a little — for a while, in one department of life. Godliness is 'of value in every way', and then he gives the reason: it 'holds promise for the present life and also for the life to come.'

There is the difference, and it is the honest one. Every athlete knows that whatever he builds will eventually be taken from him; the strongest body on earth is on a schedule. Training for godliness is the only regime whose results survive the body it was performed in.

But do not miss the first half of the promise: godliness holds promise for the present life, not only the next. Paul is not offering a religion that pays out solely after death. A life ordered toward God is better now — in the plain sense that self-control beats being ruled by appetite, that a clear conscience sleeps better, that love makes richer company than resentment. He will guard this against the false teachers who imagined godliness was a means of financial gain (6:5), but he does not withdraw it.

And the practical force is in the word 'training', which the comparison keeps alive. Nobody expects a body to change through good intentions or a single decision. It changes through repetition, when you do not feel like it, over years. Paul is saying the soul works the same way — which is more encouraging than it first sounds, because it means progress does not depend on inspiration.

verseByVerse.quote: The saying is trustworthy and deserving of full acceptance. For to this end we toil and strive, because we have our hope set on the living God, who is the Savior of all people, especially of those who believe.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'The saying is trustworthy and deserving of full acceptance' — the third of the five formulas, and here it most likely points back to what has just been said about godliness holding promise for this life and the next.

'For to this end we toil and strive.' Two hard words. The first is kopiao, labour to exhaustion; the second is the athletic agonizomai, to contend in the arena. The gymnasium image from verse 7 is still running, and Paul puts himself in it. He is not prescribing a discipline he watches other people perform.

'Because we have our hope set on the living God.' There is the fuel, and note that it is hope rather than duty. The reason a man will work himself to exhaustion for godliness is that he expects something — and the God he expects it from is alive, unlike the one in the great temple down the road.

Then a phrase that has caused genuine difficulty: God 'is the Saviour of all people, especially of those who believe.'

It cannot mean everyone is finally saved; this letter has just spoken of men departing from the faith, and the New Testament everywhere assumes a real division. Nor is 'especially' a way of saying believers get a better version of the same thing.

The likeliest sense turns on the breadth of the word saviour, which in Scripture covers rescue and preservation as well as eternal salvation. God is the preserver of every living thing — he sends rain on the just and the unjust, sustains people who never acknowledge him, and every breath any human being draws is his gift. That is a real saving activity and it extends to all. And especially — in a fuller and final sense — to those who believe, for whom the temporal preservation opens into eternal life.

Read that way the verse fits its context exactly. Paul has been defending the goodness of creation against men who despised it. The God who feeds and sustains everybody is the same God who saves believers, and it is one generosity running at two depths.

verseByVerse.quote: Command and teach these things. Let no one despise you for your youth, but set the believers an example in speech, in conduct, in love, in faith, in purity.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Command and teach these things.' Two verbs, and the first is stronger than we expect for a young man in a difficult post. Timothy is not merely to suggest or commend. He is to command — because, as chapter 1 established, the instructions were never his in the first place.

'Let no one despise you for your youth.' The word means to think down on, to look at someone and mentally file them lower. Timothy was probably in his thirties, which in a culture that gave authority to age was young for the job he had — and the congregation contained older men, some of whom wanted his role.

Note the shape of the instruction, because it is not what it first appears. Paul does not tell Timothy to assert himself, or to remind people of his commission, or to be tougher. Nor does he tell the church to respect him. He tells Timothy to be so obviously worth following that contempt has nothing to feed on: 'but set the believers an example.'

The word is typos, the stamp or die that leaves its impression. Authority in this letter is not claimed, it is displayed — the same logic as Paul's own night-and-day work at Thessalonica, and the same word he used of it (2 Thess 3:9).

Then five areas, and their order repays attention. 'In speech' — what comes out of his mouth, the most public thing about him. 'In conduct' — the whole visible manner of life. 'In love' — the goal named back at 1:5. 'In faith' — his actual trust in God, which people can see more than we assume. And 'in purity', which is the private one, and the last, and the foundation of the other four.

They run from the most visible to the least, and the least visible is where it is actually decided. A young minister cannot make a congregation respect him. What he can do is give them nothing to point at — and Paul's counsel to a man being looked down on is not to fight for standing but to earn it where nobody is watching.

verseByVerse.quote: Until I come, devote yourself to the public reading of Scripture, to exhortation, to teaching. Do not neglect the gift you have, which was given you by prophecy when the council of elders laid their hands on you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Until I come, devote yourself to the public reading of Scripture, to exhortation, to teaching.'

Three activities, and the first tells us something easily lost. Most Christians could not read, and copies of the Scriptures were expensive and scarce. For a congregation, hearing the Bible meant one literate person standing up and reading it aloud to everybody — and that is what Paul puts first. Before explanation, before application: the text itself, read out.

This is the synagogue pattern carried into the church, and it means Paul assumed Old Testament Scripture was being read publicly in a Gentile congregation as a matter of course. A church's primary act of teaching is letting the Bible be heard.

Then 'exhortation' — paraklesis, the coming-alongside word: urging, encouraging, applying. And 'teaching' — explaining, giving the sense. Read, explain, apply. It is the shape of Christian ministry in three words, and it has not changed.

'Do not neglect the gift you have.' The verb means to be careless of, to let something lie unused. Which tells us a gift can be possessed and wasted — Paul does not say Timothy might lose it, but that he might leave it in a drawer.

The gift 'was given you by prophecy when the council of elders laid their hands on you.' Two things had happened at that commissioning: something was spoken over him (the prophecies of 1:18), and a group of men put their hands on him. The laying on of hands was the Old Testament gesture of transfer and identification, and here it is the church's public act of setting a man apart.

Note who did it: a council of elders, plural. Timothy's ministry was not self-generated and not conferred by Paul alone. A body of men had publicly identified themselves with him — which is exactly the thing to remember when the job is going badly and a man wonders whether he was ever meant to be doing it.

verseByVerse.quote: Practice these things, immerse yourself in them, so that all may see your progress. Keep a close watch on yourself and on the teaching. Persist in this, for by so doing you will save both yourself and your hearers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Practice these things, immerse yourself in them.' The second verb is literally 'be in these things' — be found inside them, live there. The old translations had 'give thyself wholly to them', which catches it.

'So that all may see your progress.' The word is the pioneer word prokope — the engineers cutting a road ahead of an army. And Paul expects it to be visible. That is a remarkable thing to say to a minister, and a searching one: the congregation should be able to see that he is a better man than he was five years ago.

It also settles something about Timothy's standing. He is not presented as a finished article who has arrived and now dispenses. He is a man still under construction, and Paul wants the building work on public view. A leader who cannot be seen to be growing is teaching his people that growth stops somewhere.

'Keep a close watch on yourself and on the teaching.' Two objects, in that order, and the order is the point. His own life first, then his doctrine. A man may guard his theology with great care while his character quietly comes apart, and this letter has already shown where that ends — the conscience goes, and the doctrine follows it down (1:19).

But Paul will not let it collapse into one either. Character without sound teaching is no use to a congregation, and sound teaching from a corrupt man is a weapon in the wrong hands. Both, watched closely, permanently.

'Persist in this, for by so doing you will save both yourself and your hearers.' The last clause sounds startling and needs stating carefully: no minister saves anybody. Paul has said there is one mediator (2:5). What he means is what Scripture regularly means by such language — God saves people through means, and the means include a man who keeps watching himself and keeps teaching truly. Timothy is not the Saviour. He is one of the instruments, and the instruction is to stay usable.

5.title: Honour and Order in the Family of God
5.overview:
Chapter 5 is one of the most practically detailed sections of any Pauline letter — a series of instructions about specific categories of people within the congregation: older and younger men and women (vv. 1–2), widows of various kinds (vv. 3–16), and elders (vv. 17–25). The chapter's governing principle is the family metaphor: the church is a household, and its members are to relate to one another as members of a family, with the honesty, dignity, and mutual care that family relationships require.

The extended instruction on widows (vv. 3–16) is the longest treatment of a specific social situation in the Pastoral Epistles and reflects the real demographic complexity of the early church. The church had apparently established an official 'order' of widows who were supported by the community and who in return gave themselves to prayer and ministry. Paul's instruction refines this: not all widows qualify for the list; younger widows should remarry and manage households; the burden of supporting widows should fall first on their families, not on the church. These are not harsh distinctions but wise stewardship — protecting the community's resources for those who genuinely have no other provision.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Timothy is not to rebuke an older man sharply but to encourage him as a father, and younger men as brothers (v.1); older women as mothers, younger women as sisters, in all purity (v.2).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Church as Household, in Practice

This is 3:15 turned into method. If the church is the household of God, then people are treated as what they actually are — and the family frame carries real content. You do correct your father, but carefully, and never in public. You are frank with a brother in a way you are not with a stranger. The rule cuts against both failures available to a young leader at once: the harshness that treats a congregation as subordinates, and the deference that never says anything.

The verb Paul forbids means to strike at with words — a sharp, public reproof. He does not say older men never need correcting; he rules out one way of doing it, and the temptation he is guarding against is specific. A young man in authority who is not being taken seriously (4:12) will be tempted to compensate by being harder than the case requires.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Timothy was young, holding an office some older men wanted, in a church with entrenched trouble. Every instruction here is shaped by that.

Now: 'In all purity' is added to one category only, and Paul is being a realist without fuss: a young minister doing pastoral work with young women is in a situation that has destroyed many ministries. But note the safeguard he gives — not distance, but a relationship. As sisters. A man does not have to invent boundaries with his sister; he already knows what is unthinkable. That protects the women, protects him, and does not require him to treat half his congregation as a hazard.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not rebuke an older man but encourage him as you would a father, younger men as brothers, older women as mothers, younger women as sisters, in all purity.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Do not rebuke an older man but encourage him as you would a father.' The first verb means to strike at with words — a sharp, public reproof. Paul does not say older men never need correcting; he says this is not how it is done.

Remember the situation. Timothy is young (4:12), holding an office some older men wanted, in a church with entrenched trouble. The temptation for a young man in authority who is not being taken seriously is to compensate — to assert himself sharply, to be harder than the case requires. Paul takes the option away.

Then four categories, and the frame governing all of them is the family: older men as fathers, younger men as brothers, older women as mothers, younger women as sisters. This is 3:15 in practice — the church is the household of God, so treat people as what they actually are.

That is not sentimentality; it is a workable rule with real content. You do correct your father, but carefully, and never in public. You are frank with a brother in a way you are not with a stranger. And it cuts against the two failures available to a young leader at once: the harshness that treats the congregation as subordinates, and the deference that never says anything at all. Neither is how families work.

'Younger women as sisters, in all purity.' The last phrase stands alone and is added to one category only. Paul is a realist. A young unmarried minister doing pastoral work with young women is in a situation that has destroyed a great many ministries, and he says so without fuss or embarrassment.

The safeguard he gives is not distance but a relationship: as sisters. That is the exact instruction, and it is better than a rulebook. A man does not have to invent boundaries with his sister; he already knows what is and is not thinkable. Paul asks Timothy to import that instinct — which protects the women, protects him, and does not require him to treat half his congregation as a hazard.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Honour widows who are truly widows (v.3) — but if a widow has children or grandchildren, let them learn to show godliness at home and repay their parents, which pleases God (v.4). The true widow, left all alone, has set her hope on God and prays night and day (v.5); the self-indulgent one is dead while she lives (v.6). Command these things, so that they may be without reproach (v.7) — for anyone who does not provide for his relatives has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever (v.8).

The roll is for widows over sixty, faithful in marriage (v.9), with a reputation for good works: children brought up, hospitality shown, the saints' feet washed, the afflicted cared for (v.10). Younger widows are not to be enrolled, since their passions may draw them to marry (v.11) and so break their former pledge (v.12), and idleness teaches them to go from house to house as gossips and busybodies (v.13). Better that they marry, bear children and manage their households, giving the adversary no occasion for slander (v.14) — some have already strayed after Satan (v.15). And any believing woman with widowed relatives should care for them, so the church is not burdened and can reach those who are truly alone (v.16).
verseByVerse.theology:
Family First, and Why

Verse 8 is among the fiercest sentences Paul wrote, and both halves should be felt. To fail here is not a lapse in a secondary duty but a denial of the faith — the same verb used of Peter in the courtyard. A man may recite the creed accurately and, by leaving his mother destitute, have denied every word of it. And 'worse than an unbeliever' is sharper still: family obligation was a recognised virtue across the ancient world, no gospel required, so the neglectful Christian has fallen below the ordinary decency of people with no faith at all.

Note also where Paul locates the piety in verse 4: 'let them first learn to show godliness to their own household.' Caring for an ageing parent is not a lesser, secular duty that keeps a person from spiritual things — it is where godliness is practised. That is the exact reverse of the arrangement Jesus condemned, where a man declared his resources Corban and left his parents unsupported (Mark 7:9-13). Spirituality here is measured by whether the people related to you have what they need.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: A widow in that world had no state provision, few respectable ways to earn, and property law that often left nothing in her hands. God's concern for her runs through the Old Testament (Deut 10:18), and the church's first administrative crisis was widows overlooked in the daily distribution (Acts 6:1). Note what the enrolled widows did: set their hope on God and prayed night and day, like Anna in the temple (Luke 2:37). The church was not merely dispensing charity but supporting a body of intercessors — buying prayer it could not otherwise afford. And the credentials of verse 10 are entirely unrecorded work: children raised, guests fed, feet washed, sick people sat with.

Now: Verses 11-13 are not severity about remarriage — Paul commands it three verses later. 'Their former faith' most likely means a pledge undertaken on enrolment, and his judgement is pastoral realism: a woman in her twenties should not be asked to bind herself for life, because most will not manage it and the failure will damage them. Note too 'they learn to be idlers' — this is not a flaw these women arrive with but something the arrangement teaches them. Remove a person's proper work and the energy does not evaporate; it goes into other people's affairs, as it did among the idle men at Thessalonica (2 Thess 3:11). Paul's remedy is not more restriction but ordinary life — the very things the ascetics of 4:3 despised.

verseByVerse.quote: Honor widows who are truly widows. But if a widow has children or grandchildren, let them first learn to show godliness to their own household and to make some return to their parents, for this is pleasing in the sight of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Honour widows who are truly widows.' The word covers respect, but here it plainly includes money — the same word lies behind the 'double honour' of verse 17 which Paul immediately supports with two texts about paying workers. This is a paragraph about the church's welfare roll.

To feel its weight you have to know what a widow was in that world. There was no state provision, few respectable ways for a woman to earn, and property law that often left nothing in her hands. A widow without family was genuinely destitute. God's concern for her runs through the Old Testament — he is the one who executes justice for the fatherless and the widow (Deut 10:18) — and the church's first recorded administrative crisis was about widows being overlooked in the daily distribution (Acts 6:1).

So Paul is not inventing a policy. He is protecting one, and the phrase 'truly widows' is doing the work: the list has limited funds and must reach the genuinely destitute.

Then verse 4 gives the first filter, and it is family: 'if a widow has children or grandchildren, let them first learn to show godliness to their own household.' The church is not the first line of support. The family is.

Note the phrase 'to make some return to their parents.' The word is used of repaying a debt or recompensing. Paul is not appealing to sentiment but to obligation: a child who was raised owes something, and paying it back when the parent is old is the settling of an account.

And notice where he locates the piety. 'Let them first learn to show godliness to their own household' — caring for an ageing mother is not a lesser, secular duty that keeps a person from spiritual things. It is where godliness is practised. That is the opposite of the arrangement Jesus condemned, where a man declared his resources Corban and left his parents unsupported (Mark 7:9-13). 'For this is pleasing in the sight of God.'

verseByVerse.quote: She who is truly a widow, left all alone, has set her hope on God and continues in supplications and prayers night and day, but she who is self-indulgent is dead even while she lives.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now Paul describes the two kinds of widow, and the contrast is stark.

'She who is truly a widow, left all alone, has set her hope on God and continues in supplications and prayers night and day.' The word for alone is the root of our monastery — solitary, without anyone. That is the qualifying condition: not merely bereaved but without family, with nobody to turn to.

And what does such a woman do? She sets her hope on God, and prays constantly. 'Supplications and prayers night and day' is exactly what Paul says of himself elsewhere (2 Tim 1:3) and of Anna in the temple, who at eighty-four did not depart from it, worshipping with fasting and prayer night and day (Luke 2:37).

Which reframes the whole arrangement. The church is not merely dispensing charity to the helpless. It is supporting women who are doing something for the church — a body of intercessors, praying through the night hours while everyone else sleeps. A congregation that keeps its widows is buying prayer it could not otherwise afford.

'But she who is self-indulgent is dead even while she lives.' The word is strong — it means living luxuriously, given over to pleasure, and it carries a note of wantonness. Paul is describing a widow with resources and no dependants who has turned her freedom into indulgence.

'Dead even while she lives' is one of the most arresting phrases in the letter. Not dying, not spiritually endangered — dead, present tense, while the body carries on. It is the same verdict Jesus passes on the church at Sardis: you have the reputation of being alive, and you are dead (Rev 3:1).

Set the two women side by side and you have the whole point. Both are widows; both have lost a husband; both have time on their hands. One spends it praying and is alive. The other spends it on herself and is a corpse that has not noticed. What a person does with unstructured freedom is one of the more revealing facts about them.

verseByVerse.quote: Command these things as well, so that they may be without reproach. But if anyone does not provide for his relatives, and especially for members of his household, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Verse 7 vanished entirely from the older text, and it is the hinge: 'Command these things as well, so that they may be without reproach.'

Two things follow from it. First, these are commands, not suggestions — Timothy is to issue them with the authority already established (1:3; 4:11). Second, the purpose is that they may be without reproach, and the word is the one used of overseers in 3:2. The same standard applied to leaders is here applied to families caring for their own. Paul is not merely arranging finances; he is protecting the reputation of Christian households in a watching city.

Then verse 8, which is one of the fiercest sentences Paul ever wrote: 'if anyone does not provide for his relatives, and especially for members of his household, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever.'

Read both halves slowly. To fail here is not a lapse in a secondary duty. It is a denial of the faith — the same verb used of Peter in the courtyard. A man may recite the creed accurately and, by leaving his mother destitute, have denied every word of it.

And 'worse than an unbeliever' is the sharper edge. Pagans looked after their own; family obligation was a recognised virtue across the ancient world, no gospel required. So a Christian who neglects his relatives has not merely fallen below a Christian standard. He has fallen below the ordinary decency of people with no faith at all — which is a public disgrace to the name he bears.

The verse deserves to be felt before it is applied, and applied without cruelty. It does not settle every hard case; some families are estranged for grave reasons, some relatives cannot be helped by any amount of money, and some carers are already at the end of their strength. Paul is not writing about those situations. He is writing about people who could and do not, and who have arranged their religion so as not to notice.

It is also worth saying plainly what this does to a common assumption. Spirituality here is not measured by devotion, insight or ministry activity. It is measured by whether the people related to you have what they need.

verseByVerse.quote: Let a widow be enrolled if she is not less than sixty years of age, having been the wife of one husband, and having a reputation for good works: if she has brought up children, has shown hospitality, has washed the feet of the saints, has cared for the afflicted, and has devoted herself to every good work.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the criteria for the official list — 'let a widow be enrolled' implies a register, an actual roll of names receiving regular support, and probably with recognised duties attached.

'Not less than sixty years of age.' A practical threshold: past the age of likely remarriage, and past the age of earning. Paul is not being arbitrary; he is drawing the line where genuine long-term dependence begins.

'Having been the wife of one husband' — the mirror of the phrase used of overseers in 3:2, and best read the same way: a one-man woman, faithful in her marriage. Not a rule against having remarried after widowhood, since Paul tells younger widows to marry in verse 14, and he would hardly command something that disqualifies them later.

Then the reputation, and it is a list of unglamorous things. 'If she has brought up children' — the ordinary work of years. 'Has shown hospitality' — opened her house, as the overseer must (3:2). 'Has washed the feet of the saints' — the lowest job in the household, given to the least slave, and the one Jesus did in the upper room.

'Has cared for the afflicted' — the word means to relieve the distressed, and it says something about a woman now dependent herself. Before she needed help she gave it, which is precisely why the church now owes her.

'And has devoted herself to every good work.' The list is summarised in that phrase, and the whole shape of it should be weighed. Not one item is public, spectacular or recorded anywhere. Raising children, feeding guests, washing feet, sitting with the sick — these are the credentials Paul asks the church to verify. A woman is put on the roll because of a lifetime of things nobody wrote down.

verseByVerse.quote: But refuse to enroll younger widows, for when their passions draw them away from Christ, they desire to marry and so incur condemnation for having abandoned their former faith. Besides that, they learn to be idlers, going about from house to house, and not only idlers, but also gossips and busybodies, saying what they should not.
verseByVerse.commentary:
These three verses were almost entirely lost from the older text, and they are the difficult ones. 'Refuse to enrol younger widows.'

The reason given is: 'for when their passions draw them away from Christ, they desire to marry and so incur condemnation for having abandoned their former faith.'

That sounds at first like a condemnation of remarriage — until verse 14, where Paul tells these same younger widows to marry. So he plainly is not against it. Something else is going on, and the phrase 'their former faith' is the clue. It most likely refers to a pledge undertaken on entering the order: enrolled widows appear to have committed themselves to remain unmarried and devoted to the church's service. A young woman who makes that commitment and later finds she cannot keep it has broken a promise — and the problem is the broken pledge, not the marriage.

Which makes this a piece of pastoral realism rather than severity. Paul's judgement is that a woman in her twenties should not be asked to bind herself for life, because most will not manage it and the failure will damage them. The kindest policy is not to let them make the vow.

Then verse 13 names the second danger, and it is entirely practical: 'they learn to be idlers, going about from house to house, and not only idlers, but also gossips and busybodies, saying what they should not.'

Note 'they learn' — this is not a character flaw these women arrive with. It is something the arrangement teaches them. Put a young woman on a stipend with no dependants, no work and no structure, and she will fill the days somehow; the houses of a congregation are open to her, and the traffic in other people's business begins. Paul saw the same thing at Thessalonica among idle men — not busy, but busybodies (2 Thess 3:11).

The diagnosis generalises, because it is not about women and not about widows. Idleness is never neutral. Remove a person's proper work and the energy does not evaporate; it goes into other people's affairs. Paul's remedy in the next verse is correspondingly practical: give them something real to do.

verseByVerse.quote: So I would have younger widows marry, bear children, manage their households, and give the adversary no occasion for slander. For some have already strayed after Satan. If any believing woman has relatives who are widows, let her care for them. Let the church not be burdened, so that it may care for those who are truly widows.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'So I would have younger widows marry, bear children, manage their households.' Paul does not merely permit remarriage; he prefers it, and the verb for managing a household is a strong one — literally to rule the house.

Set that against chapter 4, where false teachers were forbidding marriage (4:3). Paul's answer to a genuine pastoral risk is not more restriction but ordinary life: a husband, children, a household to run. He is sending these women into the very things the ascetics despised, and calling it the safer road.

The reason is given: 'and give the adversary no occasion for slander.' The church is being watched, and its arrangements can hand ammunition to people looking for it. That concern has appeared repeatedly — the overseer well thought of by outsiders (3:7), conduct that does not disgrace the name. Paul takes seriously what a congregation looks like from the street.

'For some have already strayed after Satan.' This is not hypothetical. It had happened, and the word means turned aside, gone off the road. Whatever the arrangement had been doing to young widows in Ephesus, it had already cost some of them.

Then verse 16, also lost from the older text, and it closes the argument: 'If any believing woman has relatives who are widows, let her care for them. Let the church not be burdened, so that it may care for those who are truly widows.'

The principle is stated as plainly as it can be. Every family that supports its own frees the church's limited resources for the women who have nobody. This is not meanness; it is the arithmetic of love. A congregation that carries people whose families could carry them will run out before it reaches the destitute — and the destitute are the ones the whole chapter exists to protect.

Note also who is addressed: a believing woman with relatives who are widows. The duty of verse 8 is not the men's alone.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Elders who rule well deserve double honour, especially those who labour in preaching and teaching (v.17) — for Scripture says you shall not muzzle the treading ox, and the labourer deserves his wages (v.18). No charge against an elder is to be admitted except on two or three witnesses (v.19); those who persist in sin are to be rebuked before all, so the rest may fear (v.20). Paul charges Timothy before God, Christ Jesus and the elect angels to keep these rules without prejudging or partiality (v.21).

He is not to be hasty in laying on hands, nor share in others' sins, but keep himself pure (v.22) — and he should take a little wine for his stomach and frequent ailments (v.23). Some people's sins are conspicuous and go ahead of them to judgment, while others' appear later (v.24); so also good works are conspicuous, and those that are not cannot stay hidden (v.25).
verseByVerse.theology:
A Gospel Quoted as Scripture

Verse 18 contains something remarkable. Paul writes 'the Scripture says' and then quotes two things. The first is Deuteronomy 25:4, the ox allowed to eat as it threshes — the law's kindness to animals read as establishing a principle about people, as in 1 Corinthians 9. The second, 'The labourer deserves his wages', is not from the Old Testament at all. It is a saying of Jesus, recorded at Luke 10:7.

So both are introduced as Scripture, and one is from a Gospel. This is among the earliest indications anywhere that the written words of Jesus were already regarded as Scripture alongside the Old Testament — within Paul's lifetime, stated without argument, as something his readers would simply accept. Peter does the same with Paul's letters (2 Pet 3:16). The New Testament's own writers were already treating each other this way.

Note also the 'especially' in verse 17: some elders laboured in preaching and teaching and some did not, which is the root of the historic distinction between teaching and ruling elders. And the verb for their labour is kopiao, work to exhaustion. Whatever pulpit work looks like from a pew, Paul did not think it restful.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Verses 19 and 20 must be held together. Hard to accuse — the two-or-three-witnesses rule comes from Deut 19:15 and was applied by Jesus to church discipline (Matt 18:16), and it exists because a man in public office is a target and accusations cost the accuser nothing. But hard to hide behind — those who persist are rebuked publicly, which is the reverse of the usual instinct to settle it quietly and move the man on. A church keeping only v.19 makes its leaders untouchable; one keeping only v.20 lets any grievance ruin a man.

Now: Verse 23 is a small window into a friendship. Timothy was often ill and drinking only water — a real health risk when supplies were unreliable and wine was routinely used to make them safe. He was almost certainly doing it on principle, having just been told to keep himself pure and surrounded by ascetics who forbade food and marriage (4:3). Paul's correction is gentle and practical: take a little, for your stomach. It was a good man's mistake — trying to be blameless and overshooting into something that damaged him — and Paul does not praise the rigour, he tells him to stop. And verse 25 is the kind half of the chapter's last word: much goodness goes unrecorded, like the widow's lifetime in verse 10, and it cannot stay hidden. Both columns are being kept, and both will be read out.

verseByVerse.quote: Let the elders who rule well be considered worthy of double honor, especially those who labor in preaching and teaching. For the Scripture says, "You shall not muzzle an ox when it treads out the grain," and, "The laborer deserves his wages."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Let the elders who rule well be considered worthy of double honour, especially those who labour in preaching and teaching.'

'Honour' is the same word as in verse 3, where it plainly included money — and the two Scripture quotations Paul immediately produces are both about paying workers, which settles it. This is about the church's obligation to support its elders financially.

'Double' probably means generous rather than literally twice a figure; the point is that the support should be ample and not grudging. And notice the two qualifications: elders who rule well, and especially those who labour in preaching and teaching. That 'especially' implies some elders did teach and some did not, which is where the historic distinction between teaching and ruling elders comes from.

The word for 'labour' is kopiao — work to exhaustion, the word for a man at the end of a long day. Paul chose it for preaching and teaching deliberately. Whatever else pulpit work looks like from a pew, it is not restful.

Then verse 18, which contains something genuinely remarkable. 'For the Scripture says' — and Paul quotes two things.

The first is Deuteronomy 25:4: 'You shall not muzzle an ox when it treads out the grain.' An ox walking the threshing floor was allowed to eat as it worked, and Paul reads the law's kindness to animals as establishing a principle about people, as he does at length in 1 Corinthians 9.

The second is 'The labourer deserves his wages' — and that is not from the Old Testament at all. It is a saying of Jesus, recorded in Luke 10:7.

Weigh what Paul has just done. He introduced both quotations with 'the Scripture says', and the second is from a Gospel. This is one of the earliest indications anywhere that the words of Jesus, in written form, were already being regarded as Scripture alongside the Old Testament — within Paul's own lifetime, and stated without argument, as something his readers would accept. Peter does something similar with Paul's letters (2 Pet 3:16). The New Testament's own writers were already treating each other this way.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not admit a charge against an elder except on the evidence of two or three witnesses. As for those who persist in sin, rebuke them in the presence of all, so that the rest may stand in fear.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Do not admit a charge against an elder except on the evidence of two or three witnesses.'

The rule comes straight from the law — Deuteronomy 19:15, the standard for any capital matter in Israel, and the same rule Jesus laid down for church discipline (Matt 18:16). Paul applies it here specifically to elders, and the reason is obvious to anyone who has watched it happen. A man in public office is a target. Accusations cost the accuser nothing and can end a ministry before anything is established.
