So the protection is real and it is deliberate. Timothy is not to admit the charge — not to open proceedings at all — on the word of one person. That is not indifference to wrongdoing; it is the ordinary requirement of justice, and a church that ignores it will destroy good men on rumour.

But the protection is not a shield, and verse 20 is the other half: 'As for those who persist in sin, rebuke them in the presence of all, so that the rest may stand in fear.'

Note the participle: those who persist — continuing, going on with it after being dealt with privately. This is not a first response. But when a charge has been properly established and the man will not stop, the correction is public.

That is the exact reverse of how churches usually handle it. The instinct is to protect the institution: settle it quietly, move the man on, tell nobody. Paul's instruction is that an elder who persists in sin is rebuked in front of everyone — precisely because his position was public, and because of the stated purpose: 'so that the rest may stand in fear.'

Hold the two verses together and you have a workable and demanding standard. Hard to accuse, and hard to hide behind. A church that keeps only verse 19 becomes a place where leaders are untouchable; one that keeps only verse 20 becomes a place where any grievance can ruin a man. Both, or neither works.

verseByVerse.quote: In the presence of God and of Christ Jesus and of the elect angels I charge you to keep these rules without prejudging, doing nothing from partiality.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'In the presence of God and of Christ Jesus and of the elect angels I charge you to keep these rules without prejudging, doing nothing from partiality.'

This is the most solemn sentence in the letter, and the solemnity is the point. Paul swears Timothy in, as a witness is sworn before testifying — and he names three parties watching: God, Christ Jesus, and the elect angels.

The angels are the surprising item. Paul mentions them elsewhere as observers of church life (1 Cor 11:10), and Peter says they long to look into these things (1 Pet 1:12). 'Elect' distinguishes them from those who fell. The picture is of a courtroom with an unseen gallery: what Timothy does about a difficult elder is done in front of a congregation that includes more than he can see.

Why such weight for what is, after all, church administration? Because of what Paul is guarding against, and he names it twice. 'Without prejudging' — literally without pre-judgement, having decided in advance. And 'doing nothing from partiality' — literally not by inclination, not leaning one way.

Both are the same failure from opposite sides, and both are the natural human response. Timothy will like some of these elders and find others difficult. He will have friends, and men who have opposed him. When a charge comes in, he will know before he hears it which way he wants it to go — and that is exactly what Paul puts him under oath about.

This is one of the hardest things asked of anyone in leadership, and it is why the oath is here. Rules for discipline are easy to write and easy to keep when the accused is a stranger. The test is the case where you already know whose side you are on — and Paul's answer is not a better procedure but a reminder of who is watching.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not be hasty in the laying on of hands, nor take part in the sins of others; keep yourself pure.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Do not be hasty in the laying on of hands, nor take part in the sins of others; keep yourself pure.'

The laying on of hands is ordination — the public act by which the church sets a man apart, as the elders did over Timothy himself (4:14). Paul's instruction is about speed. Do not do it quickly.

This picks up 3:6, where a recent convert must not be made an overseer lest he be puffed up and fall. Ephesus needed leaders; the church was under pressure and its existing teachers were part of the problem. The temptation to fill posts fast would have been considerable, and Paul says no.

Then the reason, and it is startling: 'nor take part in the sins of others.' Paul is saying that a man who ordains hastily shares in what the ordained man subsequently does. Not that he commits the sin, but that he is implicated in it — because he put him there.

That is a heavy doctrine of responsibility and it deserves to land. Whoever recommends, appoints or installs is not a neutral party who can later say he could not have known. Paul's assumption is that with proper testing (3:10) he could often have known, and that haste is itself the fault.

'Keep yourself pure' then follows naturally rather than changing the subject. A man who appoints carelessly does not stay clean; the compromises attach to him. The purity in view is the same thing Paul told him to model in 4:12, and here it is defended by an administrative discipline — which is a useful reminder that a great deal of personal holiness is protected or lost in decisions that look purely procedural.

verseByVerse.quote: No longer drink only water, but use a little wine for the sake of your stomach and your frequent ailments.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'No longer drink only water, but use a little wine for the sake of your stomach and your frequent ailments.'

It is one of the strangest verses in the New Testament — a piece of medical advice dropped into a passage about elders and discipline — and it is a small window into a friendship.

Two facts about Timothy come out of it. He was often ill; 'frequent ailments' is not a single episode. And he was drinking only water, which in the ancient world was a genuine health risk, since water supplies were unreliable and wine was routinely used to make them safe.

Why was he doing it? Almost certainly on principle. Paul has just told him to keep himself pure (v.22), and this letter's opponents were ascetics who forbade marriage and food (4:3). A conscientious young minister in that environment, wanting to be above reproach and not a lover of wine like the men in 3:3, might well have gone teetotal to be safe — and made himself ill doing it.

Paul's correction is gentle and entirely practical. Not 'your theology of wine is mistaken', but: take a little, for your stomach. And note the restraint on both sides — a little, and for your stomach. This is not a licence any more than it is a prohibition.

The verse also says something about the man who wrote it. Paul has been dictating solemn instructions about elders, witnesses and the elect angels, and in the middle of it remembers that his friend is unwell and stops to say so. It is the same apostle who asked for his cloak and his parchments (2 Tim 4:13). Great theology and ordinary care for a person's body sit in the same paragraph without embarrassment.

And there is a lesson for the scrupulous. Timothy's mistake was a good man's mistake — trying to be blameless and overshooting into something that damaged him. Paul does not praise the rigour. He tells him to stop.

verseByVerse.quote: The sins of some people are conspicuous, going before them to judgment, but the sins of others appear later. So also good works are conspicuous, and even those that are not cannot remain hidden.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'The sins of some people are conspicuous, going before them to judgment, but the sins of others appear later.'

Paul returns to the matter of appointing leaders, and this is the realistic postscript to it. Some men's failings are obvious — they arrive ahead of the man, and no examination is needed. Others surface only afterwards, sometimes long afterwards.

The image in 'going before them to judgment' is of sins walking ahead like heralds, reaching the court before the accused does. Everyone already knows. And against that, 'the sins of others appear later' — they follow along behind and catch up eventually.

This is honest in a way church manuals usually are not. Paul has just laid down a careful procedure — test them first (3:10), do not be hasty (v.22), require witnesses (v.19) — and now he admits the procedure will not catch everything. Some appointments will go wrong despite proper care. He does not pretend otherwise, and he does not respond by tightening the rules further.

What he offers instead is the assurance underneath the whole thing: nothing stays hidden. Sins that do not appear now will appear later, if not in this life then at judgment. That is why haste is unnecessary as well as unwise — a man who waits is not risking that the truth will never come out.

Then verse 25 turns it round, and this is the kinder half: 'So also good works are conspicuous, and even those that are not cannot remain hidden.'

The same law runs in the other direction. Some goodness is visible and gets its recognition. Much does not — and Paul says it cannot stay hidden either. Think back to the widow of verse 10 with her lifetime of unrecorded work: children raised, guests fed, feet washed, sick people sat with. Nobody wrote any of it down. It is not lost.

Hold that, if your faithfulness has gone unnoticed, and by anyone who has watched someone else get the credit. Both columns are being kept, and both will be read out.

5.text: <sup>1</sup>Do not rebuke an older man but encourage him as you would a father, younger men as brothers,<sup>2</sup>older women as mothers, younger women as sisters, in all purity.<sup>3</sup>Honor widows who are truly widows.<sup>4</sup>But if a widow has children or grandchildren, let them first learn to show godliness to their own household and to make some return to their parents, for this is pleasing in the sight of God.<sup>5</sup>She who is truly a widow, left all alone, has set her hope on God and continues in supplications and prayers night and day,<sup>6</sup>but she who is self-indulgent is dead even while she lives.<sup>7</sup>Command these things as well, so that they may be without reproach.<sup>8</sup>But if anyone does not provide for his relatives, and especially for members of his household, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever.<sup>9</sup>Let a widow be enrolled if she is not less than sixty years of age, having been the wife of one husband,<sup>10</sup>and having a reputation for good works: if she has brought up children, has shown hospitality, has washed the feet of the saints, has cared for the afflicted, and has devoted herself to every good work.<sup>11</sup>But refuse to enroll younger widows, for when their passions draw them away from Christ, they desire to marry<sup>12</sup>and so incur condemnation for having abandoned their former faith.<sup>13</sup>Besides that, they learn to be idlers, going about from house to house, and not only idlers, but also gossips and busybodies, saying what they should not.<sup>14</sup>So I would have younger widows marry, bear children, manage their households, and give the adversary no occasion for slander.<sup>15</sup>For some have already strayed after Satan.<sup>16</sup>If any believing woman has relatives who are widows, let her care for them. Let the church not be burdened, so that it may care for those who are truly widows.<sup>17</sup>Let the elders who rule well be considered worthy of double honor, especially those who labor in preaching and teaching.<sup>18</sup>For the Scripture says, "You shall not muzzle an ox when it treads out the grain," and, "The laborer deserves his wages."<sup>19</sup>Do not admit a charge against an elder except on the evidence of two or three witnesses.<sup>20</sup>As for those who persist in sin, rebuke them in the presence of all, so that the rest may stand in fear.<sup>21</sup>In the presence of God and of Christ Jesus and of the elect angels I charge you to keep these rules without prejudging, doing nothing from partiality.<sup>22</sup>Do not be hasty in the laying on of hands, nor take part in the sins of others; keep yourself pure.<sup>23</sup>No longer drink only water, but use a little wine for the sake of your stomach and your frequent ailments.<sup>24</sup>The sins of some people are conspicuous, going before them to judgment, but the sins of others appear later.<sup>25</sup>So also good works are conspicuous, and even those that are not cannot remain hidden.

6.title: Godliness with Contentment Is Great Gain
6.overview:
The final chapter of 1 Timothy circles back to the twin concerns of the whole letter — false teaching and disordered living — and resolves them in the great climactic passage on the fight of faith (vv. 11–16) and the charge to guard the deposit (vv. 20–21). Between these bookends, Paul addresses slaves and masters (vv. 1–2), the false teachers' love of money (vv. 3–10), Timothy's personal charge as a man of God (vv. 11–16), and instructions for the wealthy (vv. 17–19).

The centrepiece of the chapter — and perhaps of the whole letter — is vv. 6–10 and their theological inversion of the false teachers' motto: they had apparently taught that 'godliness is a means of gain' (v. 5). Paul turns this inside out: 'godliness with contentment is great gain' (v. 6). The gain is not financial; it is the deep, settled sufficiency of a person who has found in God what the world cannot provide and therefore needs nothing more than food and clothing and the God who gives both.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Slaves under a yoke are to regard their masters as worthy of all honour, so that God's name and the teaching are not reviled (v.1); and those with believing masters must not be disrespectful because they are brothers, but serve all the better, since those who benefit are believers and beloved (v.2).
verseByVerse.theology:
What Paul Does and Does Not Say

Perhaps a third of a city like Ephesus was enslaved. Slaves were in the congregations, some owned by fellow Christians, and a movement calling for immediate abolition would have been crushed as sedition within a year, its members killed and the gospel with them.

What Paul does instead is slower and, in the long run, fatal to the institution. The slave is not told to obey because his owner deserves it; he is given a reason that has nothing to do with his master's rights — the reputation of God is, astonishingly, in his hands. And the picture is only complete alongside what Paul says elsewhere: he lists slave-traders among the lawless in this very letter (1:10); he tells masters they have a Master in heaven who shows no partiality (Eph 6:9; Col 4:1); he tells a slave to take freedom if he can get it (1 Cor 7:21); and he sends a runaway back as 'no longer as a bondservant but more than a bondservant, as a beloved brother' (Philem 16) — a request no slaveholding society could absorb.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Verse 2 addresses a real problem that had arisen. Some slaves with Christian masters had reasoned, understandably, that equality in Christ dissolved the old arrangement. Paul does not deny the equality — he affirms it in the same breath, calling the master a brother, 'believers and beloved' — but says it should produce better service rather than worse.

Now: It should be said plainly that the strategy took far too long, and that Christians defended slavery for centuries by quoting verses like this one while ignoring 1:10 and Philemon. But when abolition finally came, it came largely from people arguing from this book — because a principle had been planted inside the institution that eventually dissolved it.

verseByVerse.quote: Let all who are under a yoke as bondservants regard their own masters as worthy of all honor, so that the name of God and the teaching may not be reviled. Those who have believing masters must not be disrespectful on the ground that they are brothers; rather they must serve all the better since those who benefit by their good service are believers and beloved.
verseByVerse.commentary:
These two verses need honest handling, because the New Testament's treatment of slavery is one of the things people most often hold against it.

Begin with the scale of the institution. Perhaps a third of the population of a city like Ephesus was enslaved. Slaves were in the congregations — some of them, as verse 2 shows, owned by fellow Christians — and a movement calling for immediate abolition would have been crushed as sedition within a year, with its members killed and the gospel extinguished with them.

What Paul does instead is slower and, in the long run, fatal to the institution. He gives the slave a reason for his conduct that has nothing to do with his master's rights: 'so that the name of God and the teaching may not be reviled.' The man is not told to obey because his owner deserves it. He is told that he is a witness — that the reputation of God is, astonishingly, in the hands of a slave.

Then verse 2 addresses a real problem that had evidently arisen: slaves with believing masters 'must not be disrespectful on the ground that they are brothers.' Some had reasoned, quite understandably, that equality in Christ meant the old arrangement no longer bound them. Paul's answer is not to deny the equality — he affirms it in the same breath, calling the master a brother, 'believers and beloved' — but to say it should produce better service rather than worse.

Now hold this alongside what Paul says elsewhere, or the picture is distorted. He lists slave-traders among the lawless in this very letter (1:10). He tells masters they have a Master in heaven who shows no partiality (Eph 6:9; Col 4:1). He tells a slave to take freedom if he can get it (1 Cor 7:21). And he sends a runaway back to his owner as 'no longer as a bondservant but more than a bondservant, as a beloved brother' (Philem 16), which is a request no slaveholding society could absorb.

That is the strategy: not a revolt that would have been drowned in blood, but a principle planted inside the institution that would eventually dissolve it. It took far too long, and Christians defended slavery for centuries by quoting verses like this one while ignoring 1:10 and Philemon. But when abolition finally came, it came largely from people arguing from this book.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Anyone teaching a different doctrine, out of step with the sound words of the Lord Jesus and the teaching that accords with godliness (v.3), is puffed up and understands nothing, with a diseased craving for controversy and quarrels about words — producing envy, dissension, slander and evil suspicions (v.4), constant friction among people deprived of the truth, who imagine godliness is a means of gain (v.5).

But godliness with contentment is great gain (v.6), for we brought nothing in and can take nothing out (v.7); with food and clothing we will be content (v.8). Those who desire to be rich fall into temptation and a snare, and many desires that plunge them into ruin (v.9) — for the love of money is a root of all kinds of evils, and craving it has made some wander from the faith and pierce themselves with many pangs (v.10).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Root Beneath the Quarrels

Paul traces the Ephesian error to its bottom, and it turns out not to be intellectual. The last words of verse 5 give it away: 'imagining that godliness is a means of gain.' Beneath the genealogies and the quarrels about words was a business — these men had discovered that religion pays, that a reputation for spiritual insight brings money, standing and a following. That remains the most reliable question to ask of a teacher whose doctrine seems off: not only is this true, but what does he get out of it?

Note also what Paul lists as the fruit of bad teaching in verse 4 — envy, dissension, slander, evil suspicions, friction. Five items, and not one is a doctrinal error. They are all relational damage. A congregation where people suspect each other and cannot stop arguing has a teaching problem, whatever is on its statement of faith.

And verse 10 is famously misquoted. It is not money but the love of it; not the root but a root — pride and lust manage without it; and it produces all kinds of evils rather than all evils. The point is variety. Money-love has no characteristic sin of its own; it enables every sin, which is precisely what makes it so dangerous.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Paul takes the false teachers' own word and turns it inside out. They wanted gain; he grants there is real profit here and attaches it to the thing they had no interest in — autarkeia, the Stoic word for self-sufficiency, filled with different content: having enough because of who supplies you.

Now: Verse 8 is uncomfortable and should not be softened into a general commendation of simplicity. Paul sets the bar at food and covering — survival. He is not saying it is wrong to have more, and rules out asceticism outright in verse 17. He is saying everything above that is surplus, and that a Christian should know it is surplus. The real test is not income: anyone can name a figure at which they would be content, and the honest question is whether contentment arrived when the last increase did. If it did not, it will not arrive with the next one. Note too that verse 9 warns not the rich but those who desire to be — a condition available at every income.

verseByVerse.quote: If anyone teaches a different doctrine and does not agree with the sound words of our Lord Jesus Christ and the teaching that accords with godliness, he is puffed up with conceit and understands nothing. He has an unhealthy craving for controversy and for quarrels about words, which produce envy, dissension, slander, evil suspicions, and constant friction among people who are depraved in mind and deprived of the truth, imagining that godliness is a means of gain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul returns to the false teachers one last time, and now he traces their error to its root — which turns out not to be intellectual at all.

The standard is set first: 'the sound words of our Lord Jesus Christ and the teaching that accords with godliness.' Sound is the medical word again — healthy, wholesome. And note the test: teaching is measured by whether it accords with godliness, by what kind of life it produces. That has been the letter's yardstick since 1:5.

Then the diagnosis: 'he is puffed up with conceit and understands nothing.' The inflation word again (3:6) — swollen with air. And the pairing is deliberate and devastating: maximum self-regard, zero comprehension. The two go together more often than not.

'He has an unhealthy craving for controversy and for quarrels about words.' The Greek is a striking reversal — the word is literally 'diseased', the opposite of the 'sound' teaching just named. Paul's picture is of a man with an appetite that is itself a sickness: he does not merely tolerate argument, he needs it. Take away the controversy and he would not know what to do with himself.

And look at what it produces: 'envy, dissension, slander, evil suspicions, and constant friction.' Five words, and not one is a doctrinal error. They are all relational damage. Paul judges the teaching by its wreckage — a congregation where people suspect each other and cannot stop arguing has a teaching problem, whatever is on its statement of faith.

Then the root, and it is the last word of the paragraph: 'imagining that godliness is a means of gain.' There it is. Beneath the genealogies and the quarrels about words was a business. These men had discovered that religion pays — that a reputation for spiritual insight brings money, standing and a following.

This remains the most reliable question to ask about a teacher whose doctrine seems off. Not only 'is this true?' but 'what does he get out of it?' Paul puts the financial motive at the bottom of the whole Ephesian trouble, and the next verses are about money because of it.

verseByVerse.quote: But godliness with contentment is great gain, for we brought nothing into the world, and we cannot take anything out of the world. But if we have food and clothing, with these we will be content.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul takes their phrase and turns it inside out. They imagined godliness was a means of gain; 'but godliness with contentment is great gain.' The word they wanted is granted — there is real profit here — but it is attached to something they had no interest in.

Autarkeia, contentment, is the Stoic word again, the one Paul used at Philippians 4:11 and filled with different content. For the Stoic it meant self-sufficiency, needing nothing outside yourself. For Paul it means having enough because of who supplies you.

Then two arguments, and the first is unanswerable: 'we brought nothing into the world, and we cannot take anything out of the world.' Job said it (Job 1:21) and so did the Preacher (Eccl 5:15). It is not a religious claim at all — it is an observation anybody can verify, and it has never once been disproved.

The force of it is in the bracketing. Whatever a person accumulates is held for the middle stretch only. Nothing crosses either boundary. And most of us, if pressed, know this perfectly well and live as though an exception might be made.

Then the second: 'if we have food and clothing, with these we will be content.' Two items. Not comfort, not security, not a modest sufficiency by local standards — food and covering. The word can include shelter, so perhaps three.

That is a genuinely uncomfortable verse and should not be softened into a general commendation of simplicity. Paul has set the bar at survival. He is not saying it is wrong to have more — he will tell the rich in verse 17 that God gives us everything to enjoy, which rules out asceticism. He is saying that everything above food and clothing is surplus, and that a Christian should know it is surplus.

Which is the actual test, and it is not about income. Anyone can name a figure at which they would be content; the honest question is whether contentment arrived when the last increase did. If it did not, it will not arrive with the next one either.

verseByVerse.quote: But those who desire to be rich fall into temptation, into a snare, into many senseless and harmful desires that plunge people into ruin and destruction. For the love of money is a root of all kinds of evils. It is through this craving that some have wandered away from the faith and pierced themselves with many pangs.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Those who desire to be rich fall into temptation, into a snare.' Note the object of the warning. Not the rich — Paul will address them separately in verse 17, and does not tell them to divest. The danger is in the desiring, which is a condition available at every income.

The verbs describe a descent. They fall into temptation and a snare — the bird-trap word from 3:7, something that closes on you before you have seen it. Then 'many senseless and harmful desires', which arrive in company, because wanting one thing teaches you to want others. And finally these 'plunge people into ruin and destruction' — the verb is used of a ship going down, dragged under.

Then the famous line, and it is famously misquoted: 'For the love of money is a root of all kinds of evils.'

Three corrections in one sentence. It is not money but the love of it — money is a tool and Paul is about to tell wealthy Christians what to do with theirs. It is not the root but a root; Paul is not claiming every sin traces here, and pride and lust do fine without it. And it produces all kinds of evils rather than all evils — the point is the variety. There is almost no wickedness that money-love cannot eventually produce, which is why it is so dangerous: it does not have a characteristic sin, it enables every sin.

'It is through this craving that some have wandered away from the faith.' Wandered, not renounced. Nobody sets out to leave Christ for money. The word suggests drifting off the path while looking at something else, which is exactly how it happens.

'And pierced themselves with many pangs.' The verb is violent — run through, impaled — and the reflexive is the sting. Nobody did this to them. The griefs money-love produces are self-inflicted, and they come to the person who got what he wanted.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
'But as for you, O man of God' — flee these things, and pursue righteousness, godliness, faith, love, steadfastness, gentleness (v.11). Fight the good fight of the faith; take hold of the eternal life to which he was called, and about which he made the good confession before many witnesses (v.12).

Paul charges him before God, who gives life to all things, and before Christ Jesus, who made the good confession before Pontius Pilate (v.13), to keep the commandment unstained and free from reproach until the appearing of the Lord Jesus Christ (v.14) — which God will display at the proper time, he who is the blessed and only Sovereign, King of kings and Lord of lords (v.15), who alone has immortality and dwells in unapproachable light, whom no one has seen or can see (v.16).
verseByVerse.theology:
Titles Thrown at Idols

Every title in the doxology is aimed. 'The blessed and only Sovereign' is said in a city with a temple to Artemis and a cult of the emperor. 'King of kings and Lord of lords' was imperial vocabulary — eastern monarchs used the formula and it attached to the man in Rome; Paul takes the highest title the political world had and says it belongs elsewhere. 'Who alone has immortality' means deathlessness belongs to God by nature and to nobody else: angels and human souls continue because he sustains them, he continues because of what he is — which answers teachers peddling secret knowledge about intermediary beings.

'Unapproachable light' is a deliberate paradox. Light is what makes seeing possible, and here it is what prevents it — not darkness hiding God but excess of brightness (cf. Exod 33:20). In a letter about men claiming special access, the point lands: nobody has seen him, nobody can, and no technique will get you nearer. Which makes 2:5 the more astonishing — there is one mediator, the man Christ Jesus. The unapproachable light came out to meet us.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: 'Man of God' is not a general compliment. In the Old Testament it is the standing description of the prophets — Moses, Samuel, Elijah, Elisha — men who stood for God against a drifting people, and Paul lays that mantle on a young minister having a hard time. And the reference to Pilate does careful work: Timothy made his confession before many witnesses in a room full of friends, while Jesus made his before a magistrate who could kill him, and did. Paul sets the two side by side without comment.

Now: The two verbs of verse 11 are the Christian life. Flee — some temptations are not to be engaged, reasoned with or managed; distance is the only reliable tactic, and a man who stays to test his own strength has already decided how it ends. Pursue — because fleeing alone leaves a vacuum, and a man who is only avoiding things will eventually be caught by one of them. Note the last pair he asks for: steadfastness and gentleness. A man dealing with quarrelsome teachers needs to be immovable and unaggravated at once — to hold the ground without becoming like the people pushing him.

verseByVerse.quote: But as for you, O man of God, flee these things. Pursue righteousness, godliness, faith, love, steadfastness, gentleness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'But as for you' — the contrast is emphatic. Against the men who imagine godliness is gain, against those who desire to be rich, stands one person, addressed directly.

'O man of God.' It is a striking title, and it is not a general compliment. In the Old Testament it is the standing description of the prophets — Moses, Samuel, Elijah, Elisha — men who stood for God against a drifting people. Paul lays that mantle on a young minister in Ephesus who has been having a difficult time of it.

Then two verbs, and the Christian life is in both. 'Flee these things' — run, the word used of Joseph leaving his coat behind rather than staying to argue with Potiphar's wife. Some temptations are not to be engaged, reasoned with or managed. Distance is the only reliable tactic, and a man who stays to test his own strength has already decided how it ends.

'Pursue' — the word is used of hunting and of persecution: chase it down. And the pairing matters. Fleeing alone leaves a vacuum, and a man who is only avoiding things will eventually be caught by one of them. You have to be running toward something.

Six things to chase, and they fall into pairs. Righteousness and godliness — right conduct toward people, right devotion toward God. Faith and love — the two that have run through this letter since 1:5. Then steadfastness and gentleness, which is the interesting pair: hypomone, the staying power that does not buckle under weight, and praupathia, a rare word meaning mildness of temper.

Those last two together are the answer to what this chapter has described. A man dealing with quarrelsome teachers and constant friction needs to be immovable and unaggravated at the same time — to hold the ground without becoming like the people pushing him. That is a hard combination, and it is exactly the one Paul asks for.

verseByVerse.quote: Fight the good fight of the faith. Take hold of the eternal life to which you were called and about which you made the good confession in the presence of many witnesses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Fight the good fight of the faith.' The verb is agonizou, from the arena — contend, struggle, strain. It is the same root as the word for an athletic contest and for agony, and Paul has used the military and athletic images throughout (1:18; 4:7-8).

Note the definite article: the good fight of the faith. Not any struggle a Christian happens to be in, and not a private battle with a besetting sin. Paul means the one contest that matters, waged over the faith itself — the deposit he will name in verse 20.

'Take hold of the eternal life to which you were called.' The verb means to seize, to grab and keep hold of. That sounds odd applied to eternal life, which Timothy already has as a gift. But this is Paul's regular pattern: what God gives, you are then told to lay hold of — work out your salvation because God works in you (Phil 2:12-13). The possession is secure and the grip is still commanded.

Then the memory Paul reaches for: 'about which you made the good confession in the presence of many witnesses.' Almost certainly his baptism or his commissioning — a public occasion where Timothy said in front of people what he believed.

Paul does this repeatedly in these letters. When a man is flagging, he sends him back to what was said over him and by him at the beginning (1:18; 4:14). That is a practical kindness. Feelings about ministry come and go; the fact that you stood up in front of witnesses and confessed Christ does not, and on the days when nothing else is steady it is a fixed point you can put your weight on.

And the phrase is about to be used of someone else. In the very next verse Christ himself makes 'the good confession' before Pilate — which tells Timothy what company he is in, and what such confessions can cost.

verseByVerse.quote: I charge you in the presence of God, who gives life to all things, and of Christ Jesus, who in his testimony before Pontius Pilate made the good confession, to keep the commandment unstained and free from reproach until the appearing of our Lord Jesus Christ,
verseByVerse.commentary:
'I charge you in the presence of God, who gives life to all things, and of Christ Jesus, who in his testimony before Pontius Pilate made the good confession.' The second solemn oath of the letter (cf. 5:21), and both witnesses are chosen for the occasion.

God is named as the one 'who gives life to all things' — which is precisely what a man needs to remember if the charge might cost him his own. And Christ is named for the moment he stood before a Roman governor with his life in the balance and told the truth.

That reference to Pilate is doing careful work. Timothy made his good confession before many witnesses (v.12), in a room full of friends. Jesus made his before a magistrate who could kill him, and did. Paul sets the two side by side without comment. Confession before a supportive congregation is real; confession before a hostile authority is the same act with the price attached, and Timothy is being told which one he is signed up to.

It is also worth noticing that Paul anchors this in a datable event. Pontius Pilate is a name from provincial administration, recoverable from Roman records. The faith Timothy is charged to keep is not a philosophy but something that happened at a particular hour in front of a particular official.

The charge itself: 'to keep the commandment unstained and free from reproach until the appearing of our Lord Jesus Christ.' The commandment is most likely the whole deposit of the faith, which he will call 'the deposit' in verse 20.

Two adjectives describe how it is to be kept — unstained and free from reproach — and both are about the keeper as much as the thing kept. A man's life can put a mark on the message he carries. And the timescale is the whole of it: not until the trouble in Ephesus resolves, or until Paul arrives, but 'until the appearing of our Lord Jesus Christ.' The assignment has one end date, and it is not in Timothy's diary.

verseByVerse.quote: which he will display at the proper time—he who is the blessed and only Sovereign, the King of kings and Lord of lords, who alone has immortality, who dwells in unapproachable light, whom no one has ever seen or can see. To him be honor and eternal dominion. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The mention of Christ's appearing sets Paul off, and the letter breaks into its second doxology (cf. 1:17). It reads like something already sung.

'Which he will display at the proper time' — kairos, the appointed moment. Nobody hurries it and nobody delays it.

Then the titles, and every one of them is a stone thrown at an idol. 'The blessed and only Sovereign' — makarios again from 1:11, perfectly and self-sufficiently happy; and only, in a city with a temple to Artemis and a cult of the emperor.

'King of kings and Lord of lords.' This was imperial vocabulary. Eastern monarchs used the formula, and it attached to the man in Rome. Paul takes the highest title available in the political world and says it belongs to someone else — and Timothy is to keep his charge until that king appears.

'Who alone has immortality.' Not merely that God happens to live forever, but that deathlessness belongs to him by nature and to nobody else. Angels and human souls continue because he sustains them; he continues because of what he is. The false teachers were peddling secret knowledge about intermediary beings, and Paul says there is one immortal.

'Who dwells in unapproachable light, whom no one has ever seen or can see.' The paradox is deliberate. Light is what makes seeing possible, and here it is what prevents it — not darkness keeping God hidden but excess of brightness. Moses was told no man may see God's face and live (Exod 33:20). The obstacle is not that there is too little to see.

And that is where the doxology lands in a letter about false teachers claiming special access. Nobody has seen him, nobody can, and no technique will get you nearer. Which makes the one line Paul has already written the more astonishing: there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus (2:5). The unapproachable light came out to meet us.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The rich in this present age are charged not to be haughty, nor to hope in the uncertainty of riches, but in God, who richly provides everything to enjoy (v.17). They are to do good, be rich in good works, be generous and ready to share (v.18), thus storing up treasure as a good foundation for the future, so as to take hold of what is truly life (v.19).

Then the last charge: O Timothy, guard the deposit entrusted to you, avoiding irreverent babble and the contradictions of what is falsely called knowledge (v.20) — which some have professed and so swerved from the faith (v.21). Grace be with you.
verseByVerse.theology:
Guard the Deposit

Paratheke is a technical term from banking and law: property placed with someone for safekeeping. In a world without secure storage you left valuables with a trustworthy man, and his obligation was absolute — not to invest it, improve it or use it, but to return exactly what he received. That is Paul's picture of the gospel and of Timothy's job. It was entrusted to Paul (1:11) and now to Timothy, and it is not his to develop or make more interesting.

Against it stands 'what is falsely called knowledge' — gnosis, the word that would name the great heresy of the next century with its promise of secret understanding for insiders. Whether or not developed gnosticism existed yet, the instinct plainly did, and Paul's verdict is in the adjective: falsely called. It advertises knowledge and has none. The whole letter is in that one verse — on one side a fixed deposit, received and handed on; on the other an endless production of new material that sounds impressive and is empty noise. Every generation faces the same choice, and the second is always the more exciting.

Note also what guarding requires. Not aggression — Paul has ruled out the quarrelsome man (3:3) and the craving for controversy (6:4). A guard does not chase. He stays where he was posted, and the thing he was given is still there in the morning.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Note what Paul does not tell the rich. Not to divest, and not to repent of being wealthy. He names two dangers — haughtiness, money's quiet persuasion that you are a different sort of human, and hoping in 'the uncertainty of riches', which is exact: wealth's defining property, for the purposes of hope, is that it might not be there. And then the most generous sentence in the letter, from the man who has just said food and clothing are enough: God 'richly provides us with everything to enjoy' — the final answer to the ascetics of 4:3.

Now: The wordplay in verse 18 is deliberate: they are rich in one currency, and Paul tells them to get rich in another. 'Ready to share' goes further than generosity — not merely willing when asked, but holding what they have as common property with people who need it. And giving is described as an investment (v.19), on Christ's own image of treasure in heaven (Matt 6:19-20). The letter then ends where it began: 'swerved' is the archer's word from 1:6, missing the mark. And the final 'you' is plural — after pages addressed to Timothy personally, Paul turns to the room. Grace to the elders being assessed, the widows on the roll, the rich being charged, the slaves, and even the men who wanted to be teachers.

verseByVerse.quote: As for the rich in this present age, charge them not to be haughty, nor to set their hopes on the uncertainty of riches, but on God, who richly provides us with everything to enjoy. They are to do good, to be rich in good works, to be generous and ready to share, thus storing up treasure for themselves as a good foundation for the future, so that they may take hold of that which is truly life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now Paul turns to the rich in the congregation — and it matters enormously what he does not say. He does not tell them to divest, and he does not treat wealth as a sin requiring repentance. He gives them instructions for handling it.

Two dangers first. 'Not to be haughty' — the word means high-minded, and it is the natural drift of money: it quietly persuades a person that he is a different sort of human from the people who do not have it. And 'nor to set their hopes on the uncertainty of riches.' The phrase is exact — not on uncertain riches but on the uncertainty of them. Wealth's defining property, for the purposes of hope, is that it might not be there.

'But on God, who richly provides us with everything to enjoy.' Stop on that, because it is one of the most generous sentences in the New Testament and it comes from the man who has just said food and clothing are enough. God provides richly. And the purpose named is enjoyment — not merely use, not bare sufficiency. This is the final answer to the ascetics of chapter 4 who forbade marriage and food. The God who gives us things means us to be glad of them.

Then four things for the rich to do, and they build. 'Do good' — the general instruction. 'Be rich in good works' — and there is the deliberate wordplay: they are rich in one currency, and Paul tells them to get rich in another. 'Generous' — open-handed. And 'ready to share', which is a further step: not merely willing when asked, but holding what they have as common property with people who need it.

'Thus storing up treasure for themselves as a good foundation for the future.' The image is Christ's own — treasure in heaven where moth and rust do not destroy (Matt 6:19-20) — and it turns the whole thing round. Giving money away is here described as an investment, the only one whose returns are guaranteed.

'So that they may take hold of that which is truly life.' The same verb as verse 12, and the same implication. What the rich are currently holding is not, in Paul's estimate, quite life. There is a realer thing available, and the way to lay hold of it is to let go of the other.

verseByVerse.quote: O Timothy, guard the deposit entrusted to you. Avoid the irreverent babble and contradictions of what is falsely called "knowledge,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
'O Timothy' — the letter's last direct address, and the vocative gives it the sound of a hand on the shoulder.

'Guard the deposit entrusted to you.' The word is paratheke, a technical term from banking and law: property placed with someone for safekeeping. In a world without secure storage you left valuables with a trustworthy man, and the obligation on him was absolute — not to invest it, improve it or use it, but to return exactly what he received.

That is Paul's picture of the gospel and of Timothy's job. It was 'entrusted' to Paul (1:11) and now to Timothy, and it is not his. His task is not to develop it or make it more interesting. It is to hand it on intact.

Then what to avoid: 'the irreverent babble and contradictions of what is falsely called knowledge.' The word for babble means empty noise. And 'knowledge' is gnosis — the very word that would name the great heresy of the next century, gnosticism, with its promise of secret understanding available to insiders. Whether or not developed gnosticism existed yet, the instinct plainly did, and Paul names it: falsely called. It advertises knowledge and does not have any.

Set the two halves together and you have the whole letter in one verse. On one side a deposit — fixed, received, handed on, not yours to alter. On the other an endless production of new material that sounds impressive and is empty noise. Every generation faces the same choice, and the second is always the more exciting of the two.

And note what guarding requires. Not aggression — Paul has ruled out the quarrelsome man (3:3) and the craving for controversy (6:4). A guard does not chase; he stays where he was posted, and the thing he was given is still there in the morning.

verseByVerse.quote: for by professing it some have swerved from the faith. Grace be with you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'For by professing it some have swerved from the faith.'

The letter ends where it began. In 1:6 certain persons had swerved — the archer's word, missing the mark — and wandered into vain discussion. Here the same verb closes the argument. Paul has come full circle, and the shape is deliberate: this is what the whole letter has been about.

Note the mechanism once more: 'by professing it'. Not by studying it or being tempted by it, but by claiming it. The moment a man announced he had this knowledge, he was committed to a position, and the faith had to be adjusted around it. Public claims have a way of taking their maker where he did not intend to go.

Then the last four words, which the first fetch of this chapter nearly lost and which no letter of Paul's is without: 'Grace be with you.'

And the 'you' is plural. Everything since 1:18 has addressed Timothy personally — O Timothy, guard the deposit — and at the very end Paul turns to the room. This letter was always going to be read aloud to the congregation, and he knows it. The elders being assessed, the widows on the roll, the rich being charged, the slaves with believing masters, and the men who wanted to be teachers: grace to all of them.

It is the same last word as every letter he wrote, and it is the right one here. This has been a demanding letter — qualifications, disciplines, warnings, a list of the lawless, two men handed over to Satan. It closes with the only thing that was ever going to make any of it possible.

Grace, to a difficult church, from a man in chains, about a deposit that had to be carried one more generation. It was.

6.text: <sup>1</sup>Let all who are under a yoke as bondservants regard their own masters as worthy of all honor, so that the name of God and the teaching may not be reviled.<sup>2</sup>Those who have believing masters must not be disrespectful on the ground that they are brothers; rather they must serve all the better since those who benefit by their good service are believers and beloved.<sup>3</sup>If anyone teaches a different doctrine and does not agree with the sound words of our Lord Jesus Christ and the teaching that accords with godliness,<sup>4</sup>he is puffed up with conceit and understands nothing. He has an unhealthy craving for controversy and for quarrels about words, which produce envy, dissension, slander, evil suspicions,<sup>5</sup>and constant friction among people who are depraved in mind and deprived of the truth, imagining that godliness is a means of gain.<sup>6</sup>But godliness with contentment is great gain,<sup>7</sup>for we brought nothing into the world, and we cannot take anything out of the world.<sup>8</sup>But if we have food and clothing, with these we will be content.<sup>9</sup>But those who desire to be rich fall into temptation, into a snare, into many senseless and harmful desires that plunge people into ruin and destruction.<sup>10</sup>For the love of money is a root of all kinds of evils. It is through this craving that some have wandered away from the faith and pierced themselves with many pangs.<sup>11</sup>But as for you, O man of God, flee these things. Pursue righteousness, godliness, faith, love, steadfastness, gentleness.<sup>12</sup>Fight the good fight of the faith. Take hold of the eternal life to which you were called and about which you made the good confession in the presence of many witnesses.<sup>13</sup>I charge you in the presence of God, who gives life to all things, and of Christ Jesus, who in his testimony before Pontius Pilate made the good confession,<sup>14</sup>to keep the commandment unstained and free from reproach until the appearing of our Lord Jesus Christ,<sup>15</sup>which he will display at the proper time—he who is the blessed and only Sovereign, the King of kings and Lord of lords,<sup>16</sup>who alone has immortality, who dwells in unapproachable light, whom no one has ever seen or can see. To him be honor and eternal dominion. Amen.<sup>17</sup>As for the rich in this present age, charge them not to be haughty, nor to set their hopes on the uncertainty of riches, but on God, who richly provides us with everything to enjoy.<sup>18</sup>They are to do good, to be rich in good works, to be generous and ready to share,<sup>19</sup>thus storing up treasure for themselves as a good foundation for the future, so that they may take hold of that which is truly life.<sup>20</sup>O Timothy, guard the deposit entrusted to you. Avoid the irreverent babble and contradictions of what is falsely called "knowledge,"<sup>21</sup>for by professing it some have swerved from the faith. Grace be with you.
